Title: AI Supply-Chain Chokepoints and the Reach of Industrial Policy
Methodology: Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI) across 6 tiers of global AI stack
Key Findings: Extreme upstream concentration: EUV lithography HHI=10000; CoWoS packaging HHI=8100; Gallium HHI=9804; Graphite HHI=8649. Downstream cloud and models are far less concentrated (HHI 1410 and 1149). Industrial policy cannot replicate full stack domestically.
Limitations: Focuses on US-China dynamics; limited analysis of Global South or Indian industrial policy initiatives

Title: Semicon 2.0 and IndiaAI Mission Drive India's Chip-to-AI Build-Out
Methodology: Administrative data compilation and program audit across 6 states
Key Findings: Semicon India 2.0 approved July 2026 with ₹127500 crore outlay; 12 projects approved (>₹1.64 lakh crore committed); 3 units commercial; C2S in 320 colleges with 68k students; 211 chips taped out; IndiaAI Mission ₹10372 crore outlay with 45000+ shared GPUs; 93.18 lakh subsidized GPU hours used by 237 projects; 20 foundation models selected.
Limitations: Government policy reporting; lacks counterfactual econometric evaluation

Title: Future of India's Semiconductor Industry
Methodology: Stakeholder consultation, economic modeling, demand forecasting to 2035
Key Findings: India semiconductor demand to reach $108B by 2030 and $200B by 2035; currently 90-95% import dependent. ISM 2.0 strategy focuses on mature nodes (28nm-65nm), compound semiconductors (SiC/GaN), and top-3 global OSAT/packaging hub. Formulates 'Becoming Indispensable, Not Imitative'.
Limitations: Focuses on broad electronics rather than dedicated AI supercomputing clusters

Title: Programmable Sovereignty: Coordinated Specialization as a Response to the N-2 Problem in AI
Methodology: Game-theoretic modeling of international technology competition
Key Findings: Formulates the 'N-2 Problem': only the US and China can achieve full-stack production sovereignty. Non-superpowers face structural dependence. Defines 'Programmable Sovereignty' as soft governance anchored by pooled compute capacity, and 'Coordinated Specialisation' as multilateral capability sharing.
Limitations: Theoretical framework; requires calibration to specific domestic power grids and state budgets

Title: India's Sovereign AI Status: What It Really Means What's Been Built What's Still Missing
Methodology: Supply chain audit, vendor interviews, cloud pricing survey
Key Findings: India has committed $1.25B, deployed 34k-45k GPUs targeting 100k, and launched Sarvam 30B/105B. Crucial paradox: 100% of subsidized GPUs are NVIDIA chips subject to US EAR export controls. Subsidized compute offered at ₹65/GPU-hour (~$0.78) vs commercial cloud ($2.80).
Limitations: Trade analysis; assumes static geopolitical alliances between US and India

Title: Achieving AI Sovereignty: A North-South Coalition for an Alternative AI Stack
Methodology: Scenario planning and South-South institutional design
Key Findings: Proposes Global South collective compute pooling, open weights architecture, and pooled procurement to mitigate reliance on US hyperscalers and Chinese closed systems.
Limitations: Policy recommendations lack hardware cost-engineering models and data centre PUE validation

Title: Top 30+ AI Chip Makers: NVIDIA & Its Competitors
Methodology: Comparative technical audit of 30+ hardware makers across data center, edge, and foundries
Key Findings: Detailed taxonomy: frontier training GPUs (NVIDIA H100/B200/Rubin, AMD MI300X/MI455X, Gaudi 3); internal ASICs (TPU, Trainium, Maia); ultra-fast inference LPUs (Groq, SambaNova, Cerebras, Tenstorrent); non-US sovereign chips (Huawei Ascend 910B/C). NVIDIA maintains >80% market share via CUDA moat.
Limitations: Focuses on merchant specifications; lacks internal yield and packaging wafer allocation data

Title: Data Centres in India: Sector Report
Methodology: Field data from 50+ colocation projects and power grid filings
Key Findings: Installed capacity reached ~1.5 GW in 2025; projected >6.5 GW by 2030; Mumbai accounts for >50% capacity due to 17 undersea cables; rack power density surging to 40-100 kW/rack for AI clusters requiring liquid cooling; Union Budget 2026-27 proposed cloud/AI tax holiday to 2047.
Limitations: Project finance perspective; focuses on debt serviceability rather than defense survivability

Title: India Just Made OT Cyber a Board Problem: NERC CIP Shows Where That Road Leads
Type: Regulatory comparative analysis (India CEA vs US NERC CIP)
Methodology: CEA notified Cyber Security in Power Sector Regulations 2026 (effective April 2027); imposes NERC CIP equivalents on all entities >=50 MW, sub-stations, and data centre feeders; mandates 6-hour incident reporting to CSIRT-Power, annual audits, and Bill of Materials (BoM) for hardware/firmware.
Key Findings: Regulatory implementation begins 2027; operational enforcement efficacy unmeasured
Limitations: Pillar 3 (Energy & Grid)

Title: Thermal Management of Ultra-High-Power AI Accelerators
Authors: Vikramaditya Sharma, Rajiv Anand, Chen Wei
Methodology: Liquid cooling modeling across 40-100 kW/rack server architectures
Key Findings: Conventional air cooling fails at rack densities >40 kW without exceeding 70°C junction limits. Single-phase direct-to-chip liquid cooling achieves thermal resistance <0.03 °C/W with PUE <1.15. Tropical ambient conditions (45°C) require closed-loop dry cooler integration to avoid massive water evaporation.
Limitations: Lab conditions; excludes monsoon relative humidity effects on external heat exchangers

Title: World Energy Outlook Special Report: Energy and AI
Methodology: Bottom-up power estimation across 8000+ data centres worldwide
Key Findings: Global DC electricity was 415 TWh in 2024 (~1.5% global demand), reaching 945 TWh by 2030. AI search query consumes 2.9 Wh vs 0.3 Wh for traditional search. Water intensity averages 1.80 L/kWh for evaporative cooling.
Limitations: Aggregated global figures; Indian regional sub-grid transmission bottlenecks not analyzed in detail

Title: United States Data Center Energy Usage Report: 2025 Update
Methodology: Bottom-up energy profiling across enterprise, hyperscale, and AI clusters
Key Findings: Detailed power breakdown: servers (55%), cooling (28%), power conditioning (10%), network (7%). Average PUE is 1.58. AI GPU clusters drive cooling requirements toward direct-to-chip liquid systems.
Limitations: US-centric climatic data; Indian ambient temperatures yield 15-25% higher cooling penalties

Title: Semiconductor Supply Chains, AI and Economic Statecraft
Methodology: Mapping supply chain nodes against statecraft tools (export curbs, sanctions, FDI screening)
Key Findings: Categorizes chokepoints into equipment, chemicals, fabrication, and packaging. Assesses weaponized interdependence and multilateral export controls across allied and non-aligned states.
Limitations: Focuses primarily on UK and Five Eyes posture; secondary treatment of Indian strategic autonomy

Title: The Geopolitics of Compute: Sovereignty, Power and Strategic Dependence
Type: Global compute asset mapping and sovereign policy comparison
Methodology: 75% of frontier AI compute clusters reside in the US; 15% in East Asia; under 3% in South Asia. Compute capacity is becoming the primary metric of 21st-century national sovereignty and geopolitical leverage.
Key Findings: Relies on publicly disclosed GPU cluster figures; private intelligence compute excluded
Limitations: Pillars 1 and 5

Title: Assessing India's Readiness to Assume a Greater Role in Global Semiconductor Value Chains
Methodology: Evaluation of India's semiconductor readiness across design, fab, packaging, and policy
Key Findings: India possesses 20% of global design workforce and deep EDA expertise, but suffers from capital costs, water infrastructure unreliability, power quality fluctuations, and lack of advanced packaging substrate ecosystem.
Limitations: Pre-dates Semicon India 2.0 announcement and 2026 fab construction milestones

Title: India Data Centre Capacity to Reach 2 GW by 2026
Methodology: Pan-India colocation facility audit and pipeline tracking
Key Findings: Capacity growing to 2000 MW by end of 2026; ₹15.29 lakh crore cumulative investment; Mumbai absorbed 94% of new H1 2026 supply; Tier IV facilities represent 43% of total stock; hyperscalers drive 85% of colocation demand.
Limitations: Commercial real estate focus; excludes compute architecture and chip-level performance metrics

Title: India's Semiconductors and Strategic Dependence: Transition to Indigenous Manufacturing
Type: Trade balance analysis and policy synthesis
Methodology: Evaluates Indian import dependence on Taiwan, Korea, and Netherlands; details Vikram-32 processor and ATMP facilities; analyzes Union Budget 2026-27 allocations and India Semiconductor Mission (ISM) expansion.
Key Findings: Focuses on consumer electronics and legacy microcontrollers; does not model advanced AI accelerators
Limitations: Pillar 1 (Silicon)

Title: IndiaAI Foundation Models: A Critical Assessment of India's Sovereign AI
Type: Model benchmark evaluation and compute audit
Methodology: Audits early Indian sovereign models (Krutrim, BharatGPT); identifies heavy reliance on fine-tuned Llama checkpoints rather than scratch training; emphasizes need for scratch pre-training on Indic multilingual corpora.
Key Findings: Pre-dates Sarvam 30B/105B and BharatGen official releases in 2026
Limitations: Pillar 4 (Models & Data)

Title: Sovereign AI and BharatGen: India's Bid for Indigenous Foundation Models
Type: Case study analysis of national AI projects
Methodology: BharatGen project funded by Department of Science and Technology (DST) led by IIT Bombay consortium. Targets multimodal foundation models in 22 official languages with privacy-preserving open datasets.
Key Findings: Focuses on public service deployment; limited technical benchmarks against frontier open models
Limitations: Pillar 4 (Models & Data)

Title: Heatwaves, Rooftop Solar and Data Centres Force Rethink of India's Power Sector
Type: Grid load profiling and peak demand analysis during summer heatwaves
Methodology: India peak power demand hit 250 GW during summer 2026 heatwaves. AI data centre power demands in Maharashtra and Tamil Nadu impose localized substation congestion, requiring dedicated captive renewable energy with battery storage (BESS).
Key Findings: Regional focus on Western and Southern regional load dispatch centers
Limitations: Pillar 3 (Energy)

Title: Defining the Intension and Extension of Nations' Sovereignty in Generative AI
Methodology: Delineates four distinct layers of technological sovereignty: data sovereignty, compute sovereignty, algorithmic sovereignty, and network infrastructure sovereignty. Highlights sovereignty conflicts under extraterritorial cloud laws (US CLOUD Act).
Key Findings: Legal and political geography focus without quantitative supply chain metrics
Limitations: Pillars 4 and 5

Title: Powered Land Full Report 2025: Global Data Center Trends
Type: Analysis of utility interconnection queues and powered land constraints
Methodology: Hines estimates 40,000 acres of powered land needed globally by 2030. Power substation lead times now exceed 36-48 months, making energized land the single greatest bottleneck in data centre development.
Key Findings: Focuses on US and European markets; India analyzed as secondary emerging geography
Limitations: Pillars 2 and 3

Title: Real-World Impact: IndiaAI Mission Progress Report
Methodology: Program telemetry and impact assessment across healthcare, agriculture, and governance
Key Findings: Documents deployment of AI solutions across public sector institutions: SMARTON voice-first education, NeuroDrishti smart assistive vision, rural agronomic advisory; confirms 58 Centres of Excellence sanctioned.
Limitations: Government impact showcase; excludes technical failure telemetry and compute downtime logs

Title: Artificial Intelligence Index Report 2025
Methodology: Tracking AI investments, model training compute, talent flows, and public sentiment
Key Findings: Tracks training compute growth (10x per year); notes India ranks 3rd in AI vibrancy, 1st in AI skill penetration, but lags dramatically in hardware compute clusters (<2% of global top-tier clusters).
Limitations: Global macro survey; does not provide country-specific infrastructure engineering blueprints

Title: Government AI Readiness Index 2025
Methodology: Scoring 180+ governments across Vision, Governance, Data, and Infrastructure pillars
Key Findings: India scores high in Vision and Digital Public Infrastructure (Aadhaar, UPI), but is penalized in the Infrastructure sub-pillar due to high hardware import dependence and grid reliability constraints.
Limitations: Subjective composite indicator weighting; does not capture real-time 2026 policy interventions

Title: Making AI Policy to Drive Innovation
Methodology: Evaluating national policy models across 25 economies
Key Findings: Compares industrial subsidy models across US (CHIPS Act), EU (AI Act), and emerging economies; warns that excessive ex-ante regulation suppresses startup compute adoption.
Limitations: Broad multi-country coverage; does not dive into specific Indian grid or fab constraints

Title: The State of AI Competition in Advanced Economies
Methodology: Econometric evaluation of hyperscaler capex and market contestability
Key Findings: Top 4 hyperscalers spent over $180B in AI capex in 2025-2026; high fixed costs create massive barriers to entry, concentrating model development in well-capitalized incumbents.
Limitations: Macroeconomic perspective; excludes geopolitical supply chain interdiction scenarios

Title: Capital, Power, and Innovation: Global Data Centres Report 2025
Type: Global colocation market census and capacity tracking
Methodology: APAC is fastest-growing data centre region with 22% CAGR. Highlights India as a primary destination driven by data localization mandates (DPDP Act) and cloud transformation.
Key Findings: Commercial real estate lens; lacks electrical and microelectronics engineering data
Limitations: Pillar 2 (Data Centres)

Title: Choking Off China's Access to AI: US Export Controls
Methodology: Analysis of US BIS October 2022 and updated export curbs on advanced AI compute
Key Findings: Details how US export controls target advanced logic chips (FLOPs thresholds, interconnect bandwidth) and semiconductor manufacturing equipment (EUV, advanced DUV) to freeze foreign AI capabilities.
Limitations: US-China focus; highlights the legal mechanism that could theoretically be applied to third nations

Title: Trade Restrictions Create New Chokepoints Across Semiconductor Supply Chains
Type: Logistics and trade barrier tracking across microelectronics components
Methodology: Documents expanding export licensing requirements for dual-use components, specialty chemicals (photoresists, fluorinated polyimides), and packaging substrates.
Key Findings: Focuses on global freight and compliance rather than strategic sovereign doctrine
Limitations: Pillar 1 (Silicon)

Title: Empowering Data Sovereignty Through AI: Smart Energy Systems
Type: System Architecture & IoT Energy Data Modeling
Methodology: Smart grid data sovereignty framework combining decentralized AI with local storage
Key Findings: Demonstrates how sovereign energy data trusts prevent foreign telemetry harvesting from critical national electrical infrastructure.
Limitations: Focuses on IoT smart meters rather than multi-hundred-megawatt AI data centers

Title: NATO's Missing Link: Shielding Vulnerable Infrastructure
Type: Security Analysis of Undersea Cables and Power Grids
Methodology: Risk assessment of physical sabotage and hybrid warfare targeting subsea communications cables
Key Findings: Highlights that 95% of international internet traffic flows through submarine cables; landing stations are critical single points of failure with inadequate naval/coast guard defense.
Limitations: NATO/Atlantic theater focus; directly analogous to Mumbai's acute concentration of 17 subsea cable landings

Title: Digital Sovereignty: Can Europe Afford It?
Type: Cost-Benefit Analysis of Sovereign Cloud Initiatives
Methodology: Financial audit of European sovereign cloud projects (Gaia-X) vs commercial hyperscalers
Key Findings: Concludes that pursuing complete autarkic cloud independence requires prohibitive public subsidies; advocates for open-source software governance and hybrid interoperability instead of pure hardware autarky.
Limitations: European regulatory environment; highly relevant comparative benchmark for India's fiscal choices

Title: Data Centers Move Center Stage: Transatlantic Energy Perspectives
Methodology: Comparative study of grid connection delays in US (PJM, ERCOT) and Europe (Ireland, Germany)
Key Findings: Data centre grid interconnect delays now average 5-7 years in mature hubs, forcing operators to deploy off-grid generation (natural gas, nuclear SMRs).
Limitations: Western focus; highlights universal challenge of grid interconnection pacing

Title: The AI Financial Fault Line: Capital Intensity in the Compute Race
Type: Venture Capital and Sovereign Balance Sheet Analysis
Methodology: Comparative financing of frontier compute clusters
Key Findings: Frontier AI models now require $1B+ in single training run capex; small and middle-income nations cannot compete on brute-force scale and must specialize in domain-adapted sovereign applications.
Limitations: Qualitative financial assessment

Title: China Has ~12% of Global AI-Relevant Compute
Type: Hardware compute tracking and stock-and-flow modeling
Methodology: China holds ~12% of global AI-relevant compute stock; domestic production of Ascend 910B/C chips offsets US export controls but suffers from lower wafer yields (20-30% lower than TSMC).
Key Findings: Focuses on Chinese domestic hardware; illustrates the difficulty of indigenous fab catch-up
Limitations: Pillars 1 and 5

Title: The Great Divide: How the US and China Are Splitting the AI World
Methodology: Models geopolitical bifurcation of technology standards, semiconductor toolsets, and model ecosystems into US-led and China-led spheres of influence.
Key Findings: Corporate consulting perspective; leaves non-aligned middle powers as undecided residual
Limitations: Pillar 5 (Governance)

Title: India Data Centre Market H1 2026
Type: Commercial colocation supply, absorption, and vacancy analysis
Methodology: H1 2026 absorption in India reached 165 MW; total stock crossed 1,500 MW; Mumbai captured 58% of absorption; vacancy rates remain under 8% in primary metros.
Key Findings: Excludes micro-level GPU rack configurations and thermal cooling engineering
Limitations: Pillar 2 (Data Centres)

Title: India Data Centre Investments Shift to Multi-City Portfolios
Type: Analysis of Tier-2 data centre investments and edge topologies
Methodology: High land and power costs in Mumbai are driving new hyperscale projects to Hyderabad, Chennai, and tier-2 hubs (Kochi, Indore, Jaipur), improving spatial resilience.
Key Findings: Preliminary investment announcements; long construction lead times
Limitations: Pillar 2 (Data Centres)

Title: India to Add 20,000 GPUs as AI Mission 2.0 Expands
Type: Official tender tracking and vendor empanelment
Methodology: IT Minister announces expansion tender adding 20,000 GPUs; empanels Yotta, Jio, Tata, E2E; establishes compute allocation portal for researchers.
Key Findings: News reporting; lacks detailed economic modeling of ongoing power subsidy liabilities
Limitations: Pillars 1 and 5

Title: Data-Centre-Energy-Use: Critical Review of Models and Results
Type: Meta-analysis of data centre energy consumption models
Methodology: Compares bottom-up vs top-down data centre energy models; finds top-down models often overestimate PUE gains by ignoring tropical cooling penalties and partial load inefficiencies.
Key Findings: Methodological focus; demonstrates necessity of localized tropical PUE modeling
Limitations: Pillars 2 and 3
